problem.title: Tuning Kubernetes HPA for Sudden Traffic Surges
problem.prompt: A ticketing API runs on Kubernetes (minReplicas=10, maxReplicas=120) with a standard CPU HPA targeting 70% utilization. When a concert ticket drop hits at 10:00:00, RPS jumps 10x (from 2,000 to 20,000 RPS) in 12 seconds. Pods saturate CPU and drop connections within 20 seconds, yet HPA does not trigger scale-up until 10:01:15. New pods then sit in Pending for 110 seconds waiting for Karpenter/Cluster Autoscaler to provision EC2 nodes, plus 35 seconds for JVM warmup and readinessProbe. By the time capacity arrives at 10:03:40 (~3.7 minutes late), 45% of checkout requests have timed out with HTTP 503. Redesign the autoscaling and surge-absorption architecture to handle 10x spikes in < 30 seconds.

spark.summary: Default CPU-based HPA suffers a 3–5 minute blind spot during flash traffic surges due to metrics-server scrape intervals, HPA sync loops, container startup, and Cluster Autoscaler node provisioning.
spark.keyTakeaway: Switch from lagging CPU utilization to leading request-rate/queue-depth metrics via KEDA/Prometheus Adapter, pre-warm capacity with over-provisioning pause pods, and protect pods during scale-up with readiness-aware load shedding.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A ticketing API (`minReplicas=10`, `maxReplicas=120`, `200 RPS/pod` at 70% CPU) jumps from `2,000` to `20,000 RPS` in `12 seconds` during a concert drop.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts 145s CPU+EC2 Lag vs. <15s Leading Metric & Warm Buffer (20k RPS Drop -> KEDA (RPS/Queue) -> Pause Pods (-10) -> API Pods (10->100)); Leading Metric Trigger & Pause-Pod Preemption (STEADY (10 pods) -> KEDA SURGE (<15s) -> PREEMPT (<1s)).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Lowering the CPU HPA target from `70%` to `30%` wastes `2.3x` steady-state compute and **still** suffers `90–110 s` EC2 node provisioning delays when a 10x surge arrives, because new pods sit in `Pending` state. Detect surges in `< 15 s` and bring warm capacity online in `< 20 s`: **Leading Metrics via KEDA / Prometheus Adapter**: Scale on `envoy_http_rq_rate` / in-flight requests per pod.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Leading-metric autoscaling + warm node buffers are essential for flash-traffic workloads: **Ticketing & Flash-Sale Drops**: Scales out ahead of queue saturation during scheduled on-sales.

learningJourney.title: Why default CPU HPA has a 3–5 minute blind spot on 10x traffic drops
learningJourney.explanation: A ticketing API (`minReplicas=10`, `maxReplicas=120`, `200 RPS/pod` at 70% CPU) jumps from `2,000` to `20,000 RPS` in `12 seconds` during a concert drop. Default CPU HPA does not even trigger until `10:01:15` (`75 s` late), and new pods wait `90–110 s` for EC2 nodes + `35 s` for JVM warmup (`145 s` total)—leaving 10 pods to drown in `503`s.

learningJourney.title: 145-second scale-out lag and cascading 503 drops on existing pods
learningJourney.explanation:
Four serial delays create the 3–5 minute HPA blind spot:

1. **Metrics-Server + HPA Sync (`30–75 s`)**: Lagging 60s CPU averages hide sudden RPS spikes.
2. **Node Boot + JVM Cold Start (`125–145 s`)**: Unschedulable pods wait for Cluster Autoscaler EC2 provisioning (`90–110 s`) plus Spring Boot startup (`35 s`).

learningJourney.title: Enterprise solution: KEDA Leading Metrics, Pause-Pod Buffer, and Surge Policies
learningJourney.explanation:
Detect surges in `< 15 s` and bring warm capacity online in `< 20 s`:

- **Leading Metrics via KEDA / Prometheus Adapter**: Scale on `envoy_http_rq_rate` / in-flight requests per pod (15s scrape) instead of lagging CPU utilization, with aggressive `behavior.scaleUp` (`100%` or `+30 pods / 15s`, `stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0`).
- **Over-Provisioning Pause Pods (`PriorityClass: -10`)**: Run a `15%` warm buffer of zero-CPU-work `pause` pods on pre-provisioned EC2 nodes; when real API pods scale up, Kubernetes preempts pause pods in `< 1 s` (zero 110s node boot wait!).
- **Fast Image Pull + Readiness + Edge Shedding**: Pre-pull images (`DaemonSet`), use AppCDS/CRaC or GraalVM to cut JVM startup from `35 s` to `< 10 s`, and apply Envoy load shedding on existing 10 pods during the brief handoff.

sectionDiagram.title: Leading Metric Trigger & Pause-Pod Preemption
sectionDiagram.summary: KEDA eliminates metric lag while low-priority pause pods eliminate the 90-110s EC2 node provisioning delay.

learningJourney.purpose: Operational control: configure bounds, failure handling, and safe production defaults.

learningJourney.title: Where surge-tuned autoscaling protects bursty platforms
learningJourney.explanation:
Leading-metric autoscaling + warm node buffers are essential for flash-traffic workloads:

- **Ticketing & Flash-Sale Drops**: Scales out ahead of queue saturation during scheduled on-sales.
- **Webhook & Push-Notification Spikes**: Scales KEDA consumers on SQS/Kafka lag rather than pod CPU.
- **Scheduled Event Protection**: Combines KEDA cron triggers (`minReplicas` bump 5 min before drop) with reactive RPS scaling.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: How do low-priority `pause` pods (`PriorityClass: -10`) reduce Kubernetes scale-out latency during a 10x traffic surge?

options.text: They keep spare EC2 nodes pre-provisioned and warm, then get evicted in <1s when higher-priority API pods schedule, avoiding the 90-110s node boot wait
options.feedback: Correct: pause pods absorb the node-provisioning delay before the spike even hits.

options.text: They process HTTP traffic on behalf of the JVM pods
options.feedback: Pause pods are idle placeholder containers that hold node capacity.
Metric speed is solved by KEDA/leading RPS metrics; pause pods solve node-boot latency.

_nextProblem.title: Tuning Reverse Proxy Buffers to Prevent 502s
_nextProblem.prompt: Your Nginx 1.24 reverse proxy fronts an OAuth2/OIDC SSO gateway and a GraphQL API at 6,000 RPS. After a product release added 45 fine-grained RBAC claims to the session JWT cookie, 6.5% of requests fail with `502 Bad Gateway`. Nginx error logs show `upstream sent too big header while reading response header from upstream` and `400 Request Header Or Cookie Too Large`. Each Nginx node has 16 GB RAM and handles up to 10,000 concurrent connections. Fix both the immediate 502 outage and the underlying token bloat without risking Nginx OOM.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
